hook_text: One summer thunderstorm uses all four parts of the Earth at once. Here's how.
clip_script: Scientists split the Earth into four spheres. The lithosphere: rock and soil. The hydrosphere: all the water, and about 97 per cent of it is salty sea. The atmosphere: the air, mostly nitrogen. And the biosphere: every living thing. Now watch a Highveld thunderstorm. The Sun heats the ground. Water evaporates from dams and leaves. Warm, wet air rises, cools and builds giant clouds. Rain pours down, washes soil into rivers and soaks into the ground, and plants drink it up. Rock, water, air and life, all working together in one afternoon. Then the water evaporates again, ready for the next storm. That is why the Earth is called a system: change one sphere, and the others change too.
visual_style: Four coloured layers peeling apart and snapping back together; a time-lapse thunderstorm over the Highveld; arrows tracing water from dam to cloud to soil to roots.
pacing: Fast naming of the spheres, a dramatic storm build, a calm close on the idea of a system.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and spot all four spheres outside your window.
